oop:1. Classes, Objects, and Why OOP Exi.title: The Four Pillars at a Glance
oop:1. Classes, Objects, and Why OOP Exi.caption: Each quadrant shows one pillar as a mechanism: a guarded field, a lifted parent, one call site fanning to many render()s, and an ABC contract hiding the implementation.

oop:6. Composition over Inheritance:5.title: Is-A Leaks, Has-A Chooses

hld-blocks:7. Replication and Leader Ele.caption: Top: one leader takes writes and streams to followers — sync waits for the ack, async may lose the tail. Bottom: a partition creates two would-be leaders; only the majority side may serve.

x="334" y="276" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fig-muted)">Overflow the backlog under load and new</text><text x="334" y="289" font-size="9.5" text-anchor="middle" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="320" y="318" font-size="11" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fig-primary)" font-weight="600">"accept() returned — what port is the new socket on?"   →   8080. The same port.</text><text x="320" y="335" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="currentColor">There is no secret second port: the listening socket stays open on 8080, and only the CLIENT got an ephemeral one (32768–60999).</text><text x="320" y="366" font-size="10" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fig-muted)">So how do 10,000 connections share port 8080? A connection is not a port — it is the 4-tuple, and the kernel demultiplexes on all four:</text><text x="120" y="386" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor">203.0.113.5:51000  → 10.0.0.1:8080</text><text x="390" y="386" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="var(--fig-muted)">fd 7 — client A</text><text x="120" y="406" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor">203.0.113.5:51001  → 10.0.0.1:8080</text><text x="390" y="406" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="var(--fig-muted)">fd 8 — client A, second connection</text><text x="120" y="426" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="currentColor">198.51.100.9:51000 → 10.0.0.1:8080</text><text x="390" y="426" font-size="10" text-anchor="start" fill="var(--fig-muted)">fd 9 — client B</text><text x="320" y="456" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fig-muted)">Any tuple differing in one field is a distinct connection. The real ceiling is file descriptors and buffer memory — not "65535 ports", which is a CLIENT-side limit.</text><text x="320" y="472" font-size="10.5" text-anchor="middle" fill="var(--fig-muted)">One thread per blocking socket stops scaling in the thousands, which is why nginx and Node ask epoll/kqueue "which of my 10,000 fds are ready?" instead.</text></svg>
